## Why This Matters

In L12 you turned 5,574 text messages into a feature matrix with **2,003 columns**. Now your boss asks the
obvious question: *"So -- what makes a message spam?"*

You cannot answer with 2,003 numbers. Most of those columns are noise: words that appear a handful of
times, words that appear equally in both classes, words that duplicate what another column already says.
Somewhere in the matrix, a small set of features carries nearly all the signal. Finding it is **feature
selection**, and it is the skill this unit's title promises: *extracting information* from data. This
lesson scores and ranks features **without training any model**; L14 then lets a model do the selecting.

## What Is Feature Selection?

> **Analogy:** a detective canvassing an apartment building interviews two hundred residents, but the case
> turns on two witnesses. The skill is not collecting more statements -- it is recognizing which two matter.

**Feature selection** is choosing a subset of the existing columns to keep, and discarding the rest. It is
the complement of L11 and L12: feature *engineering* invented columns; feature *selection* decides which
ones deserve to stay. Three reasons to bother:

- **Interpretability.** Thirty features can be inspected, plotted, and explained to a boss. Two thousand
  cannot.
- **Noise.** Useless columns do not just sit quietly -- an algorithm searching for patterns can find
  accidental ones in them. Fewer, better features means fewer chances to be fooled.
- **Cost.** Every column must be computed, stored, and maintained for every new observation, forever. A
  feature that earns nothing still bills you.

## The Filter Idea

A **filter method** scores every feature *independently* and ranks them, then keeps the top *k*. The score
measures how strongly a feature relates to the **label** -- the answer column you already have (here,
`ham` or `spam`, known for every message). No model is trained: a filter is a statistical test applied
once per column, 2,003 times over. That makes filters fast and able to scale to any width -- and gives them
a blind spot we return to at the end.

We will use three: one that needs no label at all, and two that score against it.

## Variance Threshold

The cheapest filter ignores the label entirely: **drop the columns that barely vary.** A word that appears
in almost no messages is a column of almost all zeros -- near-constant, and a constant cannot help separate
anything. `VarianceThreshold` removes them. On the SMS matrix, dropping columns with variance below `0.001`
cuts **2,003 features to 1,483** in one line -- 520 near-dead columns gone before any label-based scoring
begins. Use it as a first triage, not a final answer: a rare word can still be a perfect spam tell.

## Chi-Square

The classic filter for count data is the **chi-square ($\chi^2$) score**. Its question, for each feature:
*does this feature appear differently across the classes than chance would predict?* Take the word "free":

| | contains "free" | does not | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **spam** | **170** | 577 | 747 |
| **ham** | 59 | 4,768 | 4,827 |
| **total** | 229 | 5,345 | 5,574 |

If "free" ignored the label, spam's share of it would match spam's share of the corpus:
$229 \times (747 / 5574) \approx$ **31** spam messages would contain "free". We observe **170** -- more than
five times the expected count. The chi-square statistic adds up gaps like that (squared, scaled by the
expected counts) across the table; a word distributed indifferently to the label scores near **zero**.
scikit-learn's `chi2` applies the same idea to the count values and ranks all 2,003 features at once:

![Horizontal bar chart of the top 15 features by chi-square score. digit_count (about 65,000) and length (about 36,000) dwarf every word; below them the vocabulary words free, txt, claim, mobile, www, prize, stop (with the handcrafted exclam_count among them) and a few number-tokens form a short tail from roughly 1,000 down to 400.](assets/l13_chi2_top15.png)

**Reading the figure:** the three features *you handcrafted in L11/L12* -- `digit_count`, `length`,
`exclam_count` -- all rank in the top five, with `digit_count` and `length` ahead of every one of the 2,000
vocabulary columns. `digit_count` scores far higher than `free`, the best word. The vocabulary entries that
do rank high read like a parody of spam: free, txt, claim, www, prize. **Domain insight beat the machinery,
again.** Keep the top 30 with `SelectKBest(chi2, k=30)` and you hold the spam-indicative core; the bottom of
the list ("30", "fri", "try") scores `0.000` -- words that fall equally on both classes and carry no
information.

::: {.callout-warning title="Chi-square needs non-negative features"}
Chi-square reasons about counts, so columns holding negative values (differences, anything centered at
zero) break its math and scikit-learn will refuse. Counts, lengths, and 0/1 indicators are all safe; for
general numeric features, use a different filter score (mutual information, below).
:::

## Mutual Information

**Mutual information** measures how much knowing a feature's value reduces your uncertainty about the
label -- the *shared information* between the two. It needs no assumption about counts and catches
associations a chi-square test can miss (including non-monotonic ones). On the SMS matrix,
`mutual_info_classif` produces its own ranking: `digit_count` (0.30) and `length` (0.17) on top, then txt,
exclam_count, free, claim, www, mobile, prize.

The striking part is the agreement. Chi-square and mutual information share no machinery -- one compares
observed to expected counts, the other measures shared information -- yet of their top ten features, **nine
are the same**. When two unrelated methods crown the same leaders, that agreement is evidence the leaders
are real.

## The Filter Blind Spot

Every filter scores each feature **alone**. That is its speed and its weakness: a pair of features that
carry signal only *together* will both score near zero. The textbook case is an exclusive-or -- imagine two
0/1 flags where the label is "spam" exactly when the flags *disagree*. Each flag on its own is split 50/50
across the classes, so chi-square and mutual information both score it `0.000` -- yet the two flags together
determine the label perfectly. A filter, judging each alone, throws both away.

Catching interactions requires a method that considers features **together** while it works. That is
exactly what a decision tree does -- and it is the subject of **L14**.

## When to Use Which Filter

- **Variance threshold** -- always a cheap first cut: drop near-constant columns before anything else. It
  needs no label, but it also cannot tell a useful column from a useless one that happens to vary.
- **Chi-square** -- the default for **count / non-negative** features against a categorical label (bag of
  words, indicator flags). Fast, interpretable, model-free triage from thousands to dozens.
- **Mutual information** -- when features are not counts, or when an association might be non-monotonic; a
  good second opinion on a chi-square ranking.
- **Avoid selection entirely** when you already have few features (L10's twelve Ames columns need no
  triage), or when a regulation or scientific question requires keeping a specific variable regardless of
  its score.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Selecting on all your data before you split for a model.** A filter ranking is descriptive, but the
  moment you *feed selected features to a model and grade it* (that is **L14**), the selector must be fit on
  the training data only -- rank on everything and the test set has already leaked its preferences into the
  selection. Fit the selector like any other learned step.
- **Chi-square on negative values.** It needs counts; centered or differenced columns break it. Use mutual
  information instead.
- **Reading a ranking as causation.** "digit_count ranks first" means it *separates the classes in this
  collection*, not that digits cause spam. A spammer who spells out "oh-eight-hundred" defeats the feature
  without changing the message.
- **Dropping a redundant twin.** `length` and `digit_count` partly overlap (digit-heavy messages run long).
  A low-ranked feature may be a casualty of **redundancy**, not uselessness -- drop one twin and the
  other's score can jump.

- Given a scenario (2,000 features vs 12 features; an explanation is needed), decide whether feature selection is called for and why. 
- Given a small word-by-class count table, pick the word a chi-square filter ranks highest -- and the one it scores near zero.

- A pair of features carries signal only together: what do filters do with them, and which method fixes it? 

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why not just keep all 2,003 features? Storage is cheap."** -- Storage is cheap; *attention* is not.
Every kept feature is a column someone must compute for every future message, a knob that can drift or
break, and a chance for a downstream model to learn an accidental pattern. Most of a wide text matrix is
dead weight being hauled around.

**"Is a filter the best we can do?"** -- No -- it is the fast first pass. Because each feature is scored
alone, filters miss interactions and double-count redundant features. The next lesson lets a model rank
features while seeing them together, and the two rankings make a stronger case than either alone.

## Cheat-sheet

| Situation | Move | Call |
|---|---|---|
| Columns that barely vary | drop them first (label-free) | `VarianceThreshold(threshold=...)` |
| Thousands of count features vs a label | chi-square rank, keep top k | `SelectKBest(chi2, k=...)` |
| Non-count features, or a non-monotonic link | mutual information | `mutual_info_classif` |
| Need a second opinion on a ranking | run a second, unrelated filter | compare the two top-k lists |
| About to feed selection to a model | fit the selector on train only | (the L14 discipline) |
